dimensions.name: Target Alignment
dimensions.question: Does the question assess the stated knowledge or judgment?

anchors.2: Only a tangential aspect of the target is assessed.
anchors.3: The target is partly assessed, with material scope drift.
anchors.4: The target is directly assessed, with a minor scope issue.
anchors.5: The question precisely assesses the stated target.

dimensions.name: Answer and Scoring Validity
dimensions.question: Are the reference answer and scoring rules defensible under the stated conditions?

anchors.1: The key is incorrect or scoring is contradictory.
anchors.2: Major answer or scoring problems remain.
anchors.3: The key is plausible, but an important interpretation or scoring boundary needs repair.
anchors.4: The answer and rules are defensible, with minor clarification needed.
anchors.5: All accepted and rejected responses are defensible; scoring is clear and consistent.

dimensions.name: Question Design Quality
dimensions.question: Is the question clearly designed, without obvious clues or implausible alternatives that bypass the target?

anchors.1: Wording or answer cues defeat the intended question.
anchors.2: Major clues, implausible alternatives or unclear instructions require redesign.
anchors.3: The question is usable, but noticeable design issues need revision.
anchors.4: The question is clear and well designed, with only minor issues.
anchors.5: Wording, alternatives and response instructions work well; no material shortcut is evident.

items.title: Distinguish changes to the chatbot interface, the prompt, and the underlying generative AI model in a practical content-generation task.
items.outcome: Explain the relationships among AI, generative AI, chatbots and prompts, and distinguish their roles in practical AI use.
items.focus: Distinguish changes to the chatbot interface, the prompt, and the underlying generative AI model in a practical content-generation task.

item.question: A university office uses a chat application to draft event announcements. Staff type a request, and a server-based system produces a new draft. For each independent change below, identify the component directly changed. All other components remain fixed. Choose one answer per row; choices may be used more than once.
item.targeted_judgment: Distinguish changes to the chatbot interface, the prompt, and the underlying generative AI model in a practical content-generation task.

candidate_options.text: Chatbot interface
Prompt
Underlying generative AI model

response_rows.text: Staff replace “Write a formal announcement” with “Write a friendly announcement under 100 words.”
The office replaces the chat window with a redesigned conversation screen that sends the same requests.
The provider replaces the server's text-generation engine while retaining the conversation screen and staff requests.

scoring.normalisation: Whole-item exact match against the three keyed mappings; row order is irrelevant.

item.explanation: R1 → B: Changing the requested tone and length changes the input instructions, not the interface or processing model. R2 → A: Replacing the conversation screen changes the interaction interface; the requests and model remain fixed. R3 → C: Replacing the engine that generates text changes the underlying model, not the screen or input instructions.
provided_knowledge: The application generates new announcement drafts from staff requests.
Each change is independent, and all other components remain fixed.
limitations: This item samples the distinction among interface, prompt, and underlying model; it does not establish understanding of the broader inclusion relationship between AI and generative AI.

items.title: Identify local audience and source revisions that align a prompt with a stated brief without changing its already-aligned task, context, or output requirements.
items.outcome: Use TACOS to organise and revise prompts for a stated purpose and context, aligning task, audience, context, output and source requirements.
items.focus: Identify local audience and source revisions that align a prompt with a stated brief without changing its already-aligned task, context, or output requirements.

item.question:
A university library needs recommendations for supervisors addressing students’ difficulty finding books. The recommendations must use only the attached student survey and appear in a two-column table: problem and proposed action.

Draft prompt: “Recommend improvements for a university library where students struggle to find books. Write for student visitors. Use a two-column table: problem and proposed action. Draw on the attached survey and library websites.”

Which TWO edits align the prompt with the brief while preserving requirements already met?
item.targeted_judgment: Identify local audience and source revisions that align a prompt with a stated brief without changing its already-aligned task, context, or output requirements.

candidate_options.text: Replace “student visitors” with “library supervisors.”
Replace the source instruction with “Use only the attached student survey.”
Replace the table instruction with “Write a short briefing for library supervisors.”
Replace “Recommend improvements” with “Summarise students’ reported difficulties.”

scoring.normalisation: Whole-item exact match; selection order does not matter.

item.explanation: A corrects the audience: students experience the problem, but supervisors will read the recommendations. B corrects the sources by excluding websites, as the brief requires. C names the right audience but replaces an already-correct output format. D substitutes summarisation for recommending improvements, changing the required task rather than repairing a mismatch.
provided_knowledge: The intended readers are library supervisors.
The task is to recommend improvements addressing students’ difficulty finding books.
Only the attached survey may be used, and the required output is a two-column table.
limitations: This item samples targeted revision of audience and sources while preserving other requirements; it does not establish independent ability to construct a complete TACOS prompt.

items.title: Distinguish assigning existing text to established categories from composing new text, and recognize that a task requiring both outputs needs classification and generation capabilities.
items.outcome: Analyse required processing and results in learning or work tasks, choose suitable AI capabilities, and judge when a combination of capabilities is needed.
items.focus: Distinguish assigning existing text to established categories from composing new text, and recognize that a task requiring both outputs needs classification and generation capabilities.

item.question:
A university library has 300 written student comments and three established categories: opening hours, study spaces, and borrowing services. Staff want each comment assigned to a category and a newly written paragraph describing the main concerns in each category. They do not need estimates of future usage or suggestions for services to offer.

Which AI capabilities are needed in combination to produce these outputs? Select TWO. Treat capabilities as functions, even if one tool provides both.
item.targeted_judgment: Distinguish assigning existing text to established categories from composing new text, and recognize that a task requiring both outputs needs classification and generation capabilities.

candidate_options.text: Classification
Prediction
Generation
Recommendation

scoring.normalisation: Compare selected IDs as an unordered set; only {A, C} is correct.

item.explanation: A is correct because assigning comments to established categories requires classification. C is correct because composing paragraphs from the categorized comments requires generation. B is incorrect because the requested outputs describe existing feedback rather than estimate future usage. D is incorrect because staff are not requesting suggested services or actions. The two required functions may be supplied by one tool; combining capabilities does not necessarily mean using multiple tools.
provided_knowledge: The input consists of written comments and three established categories.
The required outputs are a category assignment for each comment and a newly written paragraph for each category.
Future usage estimates and service suggestions are outside the requested scope.
A single tool may provide more than one capability.
limitations: This item samples classification and generation selection, not the full range of AI capabilities in LO03.
It assesses recognition of a required capability combination, not implementation or output validation.

items.title: Identify when generation and validation lack the upstream evidence they require, and select local handoff repairs without replacing the workflow or transferring human accountability.
items.outcome: Analyse subtasks, input-output handoffs, capability choices, validation and human responsibility in an AI-supported workflow, judging whether they support the overall task goal.
items.focus: Identify when generation and validation lack the upstream evidence they require, and select local handoff repairs without replacing the workflow or transferring human accountability.

item.question:
A university wants accurate answers to orientation questions. Staff select current official sources and remain responsible for release. Retrieval produces relevant passages; classification assigns an office label. The drafting tool receives only the question and office label. A staff reviewer receives only the draft and checks its clarity before release.

Which TWO changes repair the information handoffs needed for factual accuracy while retaining these subtasks and staff responsibility?
item.targeted_judgment: Identify when generation and validation lack the upstream evidence they require, and select local handoff repairs without replacing the workflow or transferring human accountability.

candidate_options.text: Pass the retrieved official passages to the drafting tool alongside its existing inputs.
Give the reviewer the official passages and require comparison with the draft.
Pass the office label to the reviewer as the factual reference for checking the draft.
Have staff check the retrieved passages instead of checking the generated draft.

scoring.normalisation: Whole-item exact match; selection order is irrelevant.

item.explanation: A supplies the factual input needed for grounded drafting. B supplies evidence for human validation of the actual draft. C confuses a routing output with evidence supporting factual claims. D checks an upstream output but leaves the generated response unvalidated; accurate retrieved passages do not establish that the draft represents them accurately.
provided_knowledge: The workflow's goal, existing subtasks, current handoffs, and staff responsibility are specified.
Official sources are current; retrieval has produced relevant passages.
limitations: This item samples generation and validation handoffs, not the full range of capability choices or workflow-design decisions in LO04.

items.title: Determine when new feedback requires further evidence gathering and human review, while distinguishing calendar access from approval of a specific calendar action.
items.outcome: Analyse how an agent adapts plans to tool results and user feedback, and judge whether tool actions satisfy information, authorisation and human-validation conditions.
items.focus: Determine when new feedback requires further evidence gathering and human review, while distinguishing calendar access from approval of a specific calendar action.

item.question:
A student asks an agent to find official university presentation support and propose a personal practice event, requiring approval before calendar changes. The student checks evidence for a paid workshop, then says, “I now need a free resource I can use alone.” A new search result mentions a self-study checklist, but its page has not been opened. The calendar is connected; the proposed Tuesday 4:00–4:30 pm event remains unanswered.

Which TWO next actions satisfy the student's updated requirements and workflow conditions?
item.targeted_judgment: Determine when new feedback requires further evidence gathering and human review, while distinguishing calendar access from approval of a specific calendar action.

candidate_options.text: Open the checklist page, check access and suitability, and present evidence for student review before revising the guide.
Revise the guide from the search result, carrying forward the student's earlier evidence approval.
Keep the calendar unchanged and request explicit approval of the proposed event's exact date and time.
Create the proposed event provisionally through the connected calendar, then ask the student to verify its details.

scoring.normalisation: Compare selected IDs as an unordered set; award credit only for exactly A and C.

item.explanation: A is correct: the new requirement changes what evidence is needed; the checklist's access and suitability must be checked and its evidence reviewed before revision. B is incorrect: approval of the workshop evidence does not validate evidence for a different resource. C is correct: a connected calendar provides access, not approval, and silence does not authorise the proposed action. D is incorrect: describing an event as provisional does not remove the requirement for approval before a calendar change; later verification cannot replace prior permission.
provided_knowledge: The student requires official university sources and approval before calendar changes.
The earlier evidence review concerned a paid workshop.
The new requirement is a free resource usable alone; the checklist page remains unchecked.
Calendar access exists, but the proposed event has received no response.
limitations: Samples adaptation to changed requirements and the distinction between evidence review, tool access, and action approval.
Does not assess interpretation of calendar-tool success or failure responses or verification of a completed event.

items.title: Distinguish relevance, clarity and completeness problems in AI-generated guidance, and select a targeted revision without treating one quality criterion as a substitute for another.
items.outcome: Evaluate AI-output quality and use risks against task purpose, verifiable evidence and output-evaluation criteria, choosing appropriate checking, revision or safeguards.
items.focus: Distinguish relevance, clarity and completeness problems in AI-generated guidance, and select a targeted revision without treating one quality criterion as a substitute for another.

item.question: A university needs a guide showing new students how to submit travel-expense claims. It must cover receipts, submission steps and deadlines. Match each draft review finding to the most appropriate targeted revision. Preserve content already checked as correct. Use each option at most once; one option is unused.
item.targeted_judgment: Distinguish relevance, clarity and completeness problems in AI-generated guidance, and select a targeted revision without treating one quality criterion as a substitute for another.

candidate_options.text: Improve completeness: add the missing required information.
Improve accuracy: replace incorrect claims using current university policy.
Improve relevance: redirect the content toward the requested practical task.
Improve clarity: explain unfamiliar terms in student-friendly language.

response_rows.text: The draft accurately describes the history of university travel funding, but gives no claim instructions.
All required information matches policy, but unexplained administrative terminology makes instructions difficult for new students.
Receipt requirements and submission steps are correct and understandable; the required deadline is absent.

scoring.normalisation: Whole-item exact match on row-to-option mappings; mapping order is immaterial.

item.explanation: R1–C: Accurate background does not serve the requested instructional purpose; the draft needs redirection, not just an additional detail. R2–D: The information is complete and policy-checked, so explaining terminology addresses the audience's difficulty without changing verified facts. R3–A: The draft addresses the task but omits a required element, so adding the deadline addresses completeness. B is unused: no finding identifies an incorrect factual claim, and an absent fact is not the same as a false one.
provided_knowledge: The guide's audience, purpose and required coverage are stated.
Review findings specify what has been checked and what remains problematic.
removed_knowledge: No definitions of the evaluation criteria are supplied in the scenario; learners must distinguish their application.
limitations: This item samples targeted revisions for relevance, clarity and completeness; it does not assess the full outcome's risk, evidence-verification or safeguard dimensions.

items.outcome: Distinguish common AI capabilities, including classification, recommendation, recognition, generation, prediction, anomaly detection, retrieval, and decision support; explain the tasks they suit; and select and apply appropriate capabilities in academic or workplace tasks, checking the resulting outputs.
items.focus: Distinguish retrieval, classification, and generation by whether a subtask requires finding existing information, assigning a predefined category, or composing new wording from checked facts.

item.question: A university help desk is adding AI support. Match each subtask to the capability that best fits its input and required output. Choose one capability per row; choices may be reused or left unused. Staff will check results against official information before use.
item.targeted_judgment: Distinguish retrieval, classification, and generation by whether a subtask requires finding existing information, assigning a predefined category, or composing new wording from checked facts.

candidate_options.text: Classification
Retrieval
Generation
Recommendation

response_rows.text: Given a student's housing question and the current handbook, return the relevant existing passage and its page number.
Given incoming student messages, assign each one an existing topic label: housing, fees, or registration.
Given staff-checked handbook facts, compose a short, welcoming reply that explains them to the student.

scoring.normalisation: Whole-item exact match: all three mappings must be correct.

item.explanation: R1 → B: Retrieval locates existing source material; the requested output is a handbook passage, not a newly written answer or a suggested resource. R2 → A: Classification assigns messages to predefined categories rather than finding passages or suggesting what a student should use. R3 → C: Generation composes new wording from checked facts rather than returning an existing passage. D is unused: none of the subtasks asks for suggestions of suitable resources or options.
provided_knowledge: The scenario supplies each subtask's input and required output.
Staff check results against official information before use; the facts supplied for drafting have already been checked.
limitations: This item samples three capability distinctions, not all capabilities in the approved outcome.
It assesses capability selection, not actual tool use or learners' ability to perform output verification.

items.title: Select a change to meeting process, rather than topics, that fits the different engagement needs of agenda items and the participation pattern.
items.outcome: Distinguish a change to meeting topics from a change to how participants examine and discuss those topics; select a process adjustment suited to the stated meeting need.
items.focus: Select a change to meeting process, rather than topics, that fits the different engagement needs of agenda items and the participation pattern.

item.question: A team meeting must cover routine progress reports and a disputed scheduling proposal. Reports need only factual clarification; the proposal needs examination from several perspectives. The same two members usually dominate discussion. Which revision best addresses these needs?
item.targeted_judgment: Select a change to meeting process, rather than topics, that fits the different engagement needs of agenda items and the participation pattern.

candidate_options.text: Replace individual progress reports with a combined report and split the scheduling proposal into smaller agenda topics, retaining the usual discussion approach.
Keep both topics, allow clarification after reports, and agree ground rules for examining the proposal that give each member space to contribute.
Keep both topics and agree that every item receives a full dialogue, with each member contributing before the team moves on.
Keep both topics, allow clarification after reports, and let the two most vocal members debate the proposal before others ask questions.

item.explanation: B adjusts how participants engage, matching clarification to reports and wider examination to the proposal while addressing dominant voices. A changes the organisation of content but retains the problematic meeting style. C changes the process but assumes every item needs full dialogue, despite the reports needing only clarification. D distinguishes the agenda items but preserves dominance and gives other members only a questioning role rather than space to contribute perspectives.
provided_knowledge: Both agenda topics must be covered.
Reports require factual clarification, while the proposal requires several perspectives.
Two members usually dominate discussion.
limitations: This item samples selecting a suitable process adjustment; it does not assess the learner's ability to facilitate dialogue or formulate detailed ground rules.
No principles from the unavailable interactive exercise are assumed.

items.title: Distinguish the preventative function of establishing an open team routine from the curative function of using it to support colleagues in an existing conflict, and recognise that the arrangement can serve both functions.
items.outcome: Distinguish a standing structure that prevents destructive conflict from its use to support people in a current conflict; recognise that one arrangement can serve both functions.
items.focus: Distinguish the preventative function of establishing an open team routine from the curative function of using it to support colleagues in an existing conflict, and recognise that the arrangement can serve both functions.

item.question:
A team introduces a weekly review where staff can discuss mistakes without blame. The manager intends this routine to build openness and reduce damaging disputes. Later, two colleagues whose disagreement has stalled a handover use a review to explain their concerns; teammates help them restart dialogue.

Classify each aspect below by its conflict-management function. Choose one category per row. Categories may be used more than once.
item.targeted_judgment: Distinguish the preventative function of establishing an open team routine from the curative function of using it to support colleagues in an existing conflict, and recognise that the arrangement can serve both functions.

candidate_options.text: Preventative only
Curative only
Both preventative and curative

response_rows.text: Establishing the routine to build openness and reduce damaging disputes.
Helping the two colleagues restart dialogue about their stalled handover.
The review arrangement, considering both its establishment and its use here.

scoring.normalisation: Whole-item exact match: all three mappings must be correct.

item.explanation: R1–A: Establishing a routine that encourages openness is preventative; this aspect does not itself describe support for a particular current conflict. R2–B: Helping colleagues through their existing disagreement is curative; this aspect concerns the current intervention rather than establishing the standing structure. R3–C: The arrangement serves both functions through its establishment and subsequent use. Treating the whole arrangement as exclusively preventative or curative overlooks one of those functions.
provided_knowledge: The routine is intended to build openness and reduce damaging disputes.
An existing disagreement has stalled a handover, and teammates use the routine to help the colleagues restart dialogue.
limitations: This item samples classification of preventative and curative functions; it does not establish whether a learner can design or conduct an effective conflict intervention.
No inference about the eventual resolution of the handover dispute is required.

items.title: Recognise when monitored self-resolution should shift to facilitated communication, rather than continuing an ineffective approach, withdrawing oversight, or imposing an unnecessarily visible resolution.
items.outcome: Choose a proportionate managerial response to the described development of conflict, distinguishing monitored self-resolution from abandonment and adapting intervention as circumstances change.
items.focus: Recognise when monitored self-resolution should shift to facilitated communication, rather than continuing an ineffective approach, withdrawing oversight, or imposing an unnecessarily visible resolution.

item.question: Two colleagues disagree about dividing project work. Both initially ask to settle it themselves, so their manager agrees and checks progress privately. A week later, they have stopped discussing the division and each is waiting for the other to restart. Work is beginning to slip, but both remain willing to talk privately. Which response is most proportionate now?
item.targeted_judgment: Recognise when monitored self-resolution should shift to facilitated communication, rather than continuing an ineffective approach, withdrawing oversight, or imposing an unnecessarily visible resolution.

candidate_options.text: Keep the existing private progress checks, leaving the colleagues to decide when to restart discussions.
Arrange a private conversation to help them restart discussions, then check whether their agreement restores progress.
Announce a manager-decided division at the next team meeting, then check whether both colleagues follow it.
Suspend progress checks to give them space, asking them to report back when they have settled the division.

item.explanation: B adapts the approach as the conflict develops: communication has stalled, so private facilitation with follow-up is proportionate. A retains monitoring but does not address the newly stalled communication. C imposes a visible managerial solution despite both colleagues remaining willing to talk privately. D mistakes supporting self-resolution for withdrawing oversight while work is slipping. The source supports monitored self-resolution, facilitation of communication, and changing the approach as circumstances develop (BG012_p13).
provided_knowledge: The manager initially supported self-resolution and monitored progress.
Communication has now stalled and work is beginning to slip.
Both colleagues remain willing to talk privately.
limitations: This item samples the decision to move from monitored self-resolution to private facilitation; it does not assess the full range of conflict interventions or establish attainment of the whole proposed target.

items.title: Distinguish a time-constrained reciprocal concession from a jointly developed solution addressing both parties’ concerns, while recognising that the initial compromise can be defensible.
items.outcome: Distinguish reciprocal concessions from a jointly developed solution addressing both parties concerns, without assuming compromise is always wrong or collaboration always feasible.
items.focus: Distinguish a time-constrained reciprocal concession from a jointly developed solution addressing both parties’ concerns, while recognising that the initial compromise can be defensible.

item.question:
A support team must set tomorrow’s rota in ten minutes. Jo wants continuous phone coverage; Ren wants uninterrupted time for complex cases. With no time to test alternatives, each accepts less of their preferred allocation so the rota can be issued. Next week, they have time to examine the problem together. They challenge their assumptions and jointly develop rotating phone duty with protected casework periods, meeting both concerns.

Which interpretation is best supported?
item.targeted_judgment: Distinguish a time-constrained reciprocal concession from a jointly developed solution addressing both parties’ concerns, while recognising that the initial compromise can be defensible.

candidate_options.text: Both agreements are collaboration: each results from the two people accepting a shared arrangement.
The first is defensible compromise; the second is collaboration through joint examination and development.
Both agreements are compromise: rotating duties still means dividing time between competing activities.
The first is failed collaboration; they should delay the rota until both concerns can be met.

item.explanation: B is correct: the immediate agreement involves reciprocal concessions under a stated deadline, whereas the later solution is jointly developed through dialogue and addresses both concerns. A confuses agreement alone with collaboration. C treats dividing time as sufficient evidence of compromise, overlooking how the later solution was developed and what it achieves. D assumes compromise is unacceptable and disregards the requirement to issue the rota. The course allows compromise to be useful while encouraging exploration of collaborative solutions (BG012_p14–15, BG012_p21).
provided_knowledge: The immediate deadline and lack of time to test alternatives.
The concerns of both team members, their initial concessions, and the later joint examination and solution.
limitations: Assesses interpretation of one bounded two-stage case, not the learner’s ability to facilitate collaboration or determine its feasibility across workplaces.

items.title: Distinguish critical testing of a proposal from advocacy for an assigned contender, and recognise that equal preparation time does not resolve a major power imbalance between idea advocates.
items.outcome: Distinguish the devil advocate role of testing a proposal assumptions from an idea advocate role of presenting the case for an assigned contender, and recognise power imbalance as a limitation of the latter.
items.focus: Distinguish critical testing of a proposal from advocacy for an assigned contender, and recognise that equal preparation time does not resolve a major power imbalance between idea advocates.

item.question:
A team has shortlisted three staff-scheduling proposals. First, Maya is asked to examine one proposal’s assumptions and check its analysis for inconsistencies. Later, each proposal is assigned a presenter to make its strongest case. One presenter is a director; the other two are junior employees whose promotion the director controls. All receive equal preparation time.

Which conclusions are supported by the course? Select all that apply.
item.targeted_judgment: Distinguish critical testing of a proposal from advocacy for an assigned contender, and recognise that equal preparation time does not resolve a major power imbalance between idea advocates.

candidate_options.text: Maya’s initial assignment fits the devil’s advocate role.
The presenters’ assignments fit the idea advocate role.
The director’s authority creates a limitation for the advocacy arrangement.
Equal preparation time adequately addresses the presenters’ power differences.
The presenters should primarily identify weaknesses in their assigned proposals.

scoring.normalisation: Whole-item exact match; selection order is irrelevant.

item.explanation: A is correct: a devil’s advocate critically examines a proposal’s assumptions and analysis. B is correct: idea advocates present the case for their assigned contenders. C is correct: the course cautions against major status or power differences between idea advocates; control over promotion establishes such a difference. D is incorrect: preparation time supports case development but does not remove that power imbalance. E is incorrect: it substitutes the adverse critic’s emphasis for the idea advocate’s task of presenting a case for an assigned idea.
provided_knowledge: Three proposals have already been shortlisted.
The scenario specifies the critical-testing assignment, presentation assignments, preparation time and reporting-related power difference.
limitations: This item samples role recognition and recognition of a power-related limitation; it does not assess implementation of either technique or establish mastery of the whole outcome.

items.title: Determine the dependency chain from making a plan’s assumptions explicit, through developing and examining a counter-plan grounded in counter-assumptions, to establishing shared, scrutinised assumptions for a new plan.
items.outcome: Determine the necessary dependencies between articulating a plan assumptions, constructing a counter-plan using counter-assumptions, examining both, and developing shared tested assumptions for a new plan.
items.focus: Determine the dependency chain from making a plan’s assumptions explicit, through developing and examining a counter-plan grounded in counter-assumptions, to establishing shared, scrutinised assumptions for a new plan.

item.question: A library team is using dialectical inquiry to plan evening opening hours. Put these four work packages in the order required by the method, from first to last. Each package is completed once.
item.targeted_judgment: Determine the dependency chain from making a plan’s assumptions explicit, through developing and examining a counter-plan grounded in counter-assumptions, to establishing shared, scrutinised assumptions for a new plan.

candidate_options.text: Present both plans and their supporting evidence to the review group; probe weaknesses and identify overlooked assumptions.
Jointly pool and scrutinise assumptions, reconcile or test competing ones where possible, and use agreed core assumptions to develop a new plan.
Develop an evening-opening proposal and give its key underlying assumptions to the counter-proposal group.
Develop an alternative plan by finding plausible counter-assumptions and using them to uncover or reinterpret evidence.

item.explanation: C precedes D because the counter-proposal group works from the original plan’s explicit assumptions. D precedes A because both plans and their supporting assumptions must be available for examination. A precedes B because the joint work draws on assumptions exposed and challenged during the debate. B culminates in agreed core assumptions that support a new plan; it is not simply a choice between the original plans. The source permits reconciliation or testing where possible, rather than requiring an empirical test of every assumption.
provided_knowledge: The workplace setting and the decision to use dialectical inquiry.
Four work packages to be sequenced, without their chronological positions.
removed_knowledge: The source’s numbered sequence and explicit chronological transitions.
limitations: This item samples recognition of the method’s dependencies, not the ability to generate plausible counter-assumptions or conduct a productive debate.
It does not assess group formation, facilitation or organisational adaptation.

item.question: A college team reliably delivers staff software workshops.
